main.text: [II, 854] [col. 249] Chapter 17.
The rest of what Job says about the ostrich in chapter 39, verses 17, 18, 19, 20 and 21, is explained.

Now that we have explained in Job what was by far the most difficult point about the ostrich, [col. 250] in the rest there will be less labour and more profit. After the ἀκανθολογίαν [akanthologian], or gathering of thorns, will follow the ἀνθολογία [anthologia], or more truly the gleaning of ears. The sacred words run thus: But she leaves her eggs on the ground, and they are warmed upon the dust. And she forgets that the foot may crush them, and the beast of the field trample them. She deals harshly with her chicks, as if they were not hers. She has laboured in vain, she is without fear. For God has deprived her of wisdom, and has not imparted understanding to her. When she raises herself on high, she laughs at the horse and its rider. We shall now expound these one by one.

But she leaves her eggs on the ground] In Hebrew, כי תעזוב לארץ ביציה. The connection of this verse with the preceding one is as follows: "The ostrich exults in her wings, which she has swift and beautiful; but she is also ἄστοργος [astorgos], and neglects her eggs. She has some endowments of body, but a hard and pitiless mind." Thus כי in this place means the same as but, as in Gen 45:8. It was not you who sent me here, כי האלהים, but God. She leaves, תעזוב, is an enallage of number. For the plural had preceded: The wing of the ostriches exults. But nothing is more frequent than this enallage in the book of Job. So in this very passage: She leaves her eggs on the ground, etc. And she forgets that the foot may tread on it. And a little below, of the horse: Have you given the horse strength, etc. They paw in the valley, and he rejoices in strength. The same verb תעזוב, she leaves, though feminine in gender, nevertheless refers to the noun רננים renanim, of masculine ending. But יענים, ostriches, יעלים, ibexes, רמכים, mares, רחלים, ewes, and in this very place ביצים, eggs, although of masculine ending, are nevertheless feminine in gender ^{R1}. Further, the fact that this bird is said to leave her eggs on the ground plainly shows that it is the ostrich. For in the whole class of birds no other presents itself which is truly charged with this crime. The Indians, it is true, according to Aelian (Hist. book 14, ch. 13), hate swans because report has it that they ἐπιβουλεύειν ἐκγόνοις, καὶ διαφθείρειν τὰ ὠὰ [epibouleuein ekgonois, kai diaphtheirein ta ōa], lay snares for their offspring and destroy their own eggs. But report is not always to be believed, which

She clings to the false and the wrong as firmly as she proclaims the true. [II, 855] Nor do we need to run to the farthest Indians to learn the nature of the swan; although it is common in Holland and Britain, all the Dutch and British nevertheless deny that they have observed any such thing in the swan. Of the same stamp is what Clytus, the disciple of Aristotle, writes in Athenaeus, book 14, about the bird meleagris: Ἔστι δὲ ἄστοργον πρὸς τὰ ἔκγονα τὸ ὄρνεον, καὶ ὀλιγωρεῖ τῶν νεωτέρων, ὥστε ἀνάγκη τοῖς ἱερεῦσιν ἐπιμελεῖσθαι αὐτῶν [Esti de astorgon pros ta ekgona to orneon, kai oligōrei tōn neōterōn, hōste anankē tois hiereusin epimeleisthai autōn]; This animal has little affection for its offspring, and neglects its chicks so much that the priests must take care of them. For by the name meleagris Clytus describes the hen which we call the Indian or the Barbary hen, and the ancients the Numidian: both scarcely yield to the common hen in natural φιλοστοργίᾳ [philostorgia] toward their chicks. Nor do certain Arabs more truly lay the same charge against الحباري [al-ḥubārā] alhubara, that is, the bustard. Alkazuinius [=al-Qazwīnī, ʿAjāʾib al-makhlūqāt]: قالوا ما في الطيور اشد منه بلها يترك بيضها [qālū mā fī al-ṭuyūr ashadd minhu balahan yatruku bayḍahā] [col. 251] وتحضن بيض غيرها وفي المثل كل شي يحب ولده حتي الحباري [wa-taḥḍunu bayḍ ghayrihā wa-fī al-mathal kull shay yuḥibbu waladahu ḥattā al-ḥubārā] They say that no bird is more foolish than it, since it abandons its own eggs and sits on those of others. Hence the proverb: Every animal loves its young except the bustard. But Damir [=al-Damīrī, Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān], who has written more about the bustard than anyone else I know of, at least clears the female of so shameful a charge in these words: قال عثمان رضي الله عنه كل شي يحب ولده حتي الحباري خصها بالذكر لانها يضرب بها المثل في الحمق وهي علي حمقها تحب ولدها فتطعمها وتعلمها الطيران كغيرها من الحيوان [qāla ʿUthmān raḍiya Allāh ʿanhu kull shay yuḥibbu waladahu ḥattā al-ḥubārā khaṣṣahā bi-al-dhikr li-annahā yuḍrabu bihā al-mathal fī al-ḥumq wa-hiya ʿalā ḥumqihā tuḥibbu waladahā fa-tuṭʿimuhā wa-tuʿallimuhā al-ṭayarān ka-ghayrihā min al-ḥayawān] Othman, to whom may God be gracious, said that every animal loves its offspring except the bustard. But this properly applies to the male. For although the common proverb imputes folly to the female, yet for all her folly she loves her chicks, feeds them and teaches them to fly, just like the other animals. Someone must also have deceived Jerome when he wrote of the dove on Os. VII.: The other birds hasten to protect their chicks even at the peril of their own life, etc. The dove alone does not grieve for its chicks when they are taken away, and does not seek them. Surely there is no one who does not know that the affection of doves, both toward their chicks and toward their mates, is most tender. Male and female sit on the eggs ἐκ διαδοχῆς [ek diadochēs], that is, by turns; and in like manner they συνθερμαίνουσι [synthermainousi], warm together, the hatched chicks. And if the female returns too sluggishly after the pains of laying, the male calls her back to the nest with a light chastisement. They share the care of ψωμίζειν [psōmizein] the chicks, putting predigested food into their mouths; and when taken away from the nest, however great the distance, they return to it out of love for their offspring. Hence it has come about that some have used doves as messengers, sending them back with a note attached to the town where they had sat on eggs or chicks. Hence Oppian, book 3 [Cyneget.], verse 115.
[II, 856] Πῶς δ᾽ ἄρ ἐν οἰωνοῖσι ποθὴν ἀλίαστον ἔχουσιν Ὧν τεκέων φῆναί τε, βαρύφθογγοί τε πέλειαι. [Pōs d' ar en oiōnoisi pothēn aliaston echousin / Hōn tekeōn phēnai te, barypthongoi te peleiai.]

Just as among birds too the ossifrages have a constant love for their chicks, and the doves with their heavy moaning. That ravens, too, hate their chicks, though very many assert it, is nevertheless a fiction, as was amply proved above ^{a)}; and the eagle ^{b)} casts one egg or chick out of its nest for no other reason than that it is unequal to feeding and warming them all. But that the ostrich not infrequently leaves its eggs on the ground and neglects them, although the Greek and Roman writers, to whom the nature of this animal was not sufficiently known, do not report it, is nevertheless quite certain to me from the records of the Arabs. Damir: وهي تخرج لطلب الطعم فمتي وجدت بيض نعامة اخري تحضنه وتنسي بيضها ولعلها ان تصاد فلا ترجع اليه ولهذا توصف بالحمق ويضرب بها المثل في ذلك [wa-hiya takhruju li-ṭalab al-ṭuʿm fa-matī wajadat bayḍ naʿāma ukhrī taḥḍunuhu wa-tansī bayḍahā wa-laʿallahā an tuṣād fa-lā tarjiʿ ilayhi wa-li-hādhā tūṣaf bi-l-ḥumq wa-yuḍrab bihā al-mathal fī dhālika] When it goes out of [col. 252] the nest to seek food, if it finds the egg of another ostrich, it sits on it and forgets its own; and, driven away from there by hunters, it never returns. Hence it is described as foolish, and the proverb strikes it on this account ^{R2}. Namely احمق نعامة [aḥmaq naʿāma] More foolish than an ostrich, which the same author explains in the section On Proverbs. And the Arabs designate each of these things by proper names. بيضة [bayḍa] in general is egg, as in Hebrew ביצה, with the same letters. Hence here the plural with the suffix, ביציה, its eggs. Why an egg is so called is hidden from the Hebrews, but the Arabs derive it from whiteness. For with them the verb باض [bāḍa] means to be white. But the ostrich's egg is called by a special name تومة [tūma] thauma, which in Greek means marvel. And تريكة [tarīka] tharicha, when the chick has come out of it. And نتل [natl] nethel, when it has been left by the male, or بيضة البلد [bayḍat al-balad] egg of the region. Alcamus [=al-Qāmūs al-muḥīṭ, the Arabic dictionary of al-Fīrūzābādī]: تومة بيضة النعام [tūma bayḍat al-naʿām] Thauma, the ostrich's egg. التريكة البيضة بعد [II, 857] ان يخرج منه الفرخ ويخص بالنعام [al-tarīka al-bayḍa baʿda an yakhruja minhu al-farkh wa-yakhuṣṣu bi-l-naʿām] Tharicha, an egg after the chick has come out of it; but it is said properly of the ostrich. النتل بيضة النعام يملا ماء فيدفن في المفازة [al-natl bayḍat al-naʿām yumlaʾ māʾan fa-yudfan fī al-mafāza] Nethel, an ostrich egg full of water, which is buried in the desert, that is, in the midst of the sands. And elsewhere: هو اذل من بيضة البلد اي من بيضة النعام التي تركها [huwa adhallu min bayḍat al-balad ay min bayḍat al-naʿām allatī tarakathā] He is more worthless than the egg of the region, that is, than the ostrich's egg, which it has abandoned. The ostrich's nest, in which such eggs are usually found, is called ادحي [udḥī] udcha, ادحوة [udḥuwwa] udchua, and ادحية [udḥiyya] udchia, on account of the sand spread out all around. For دحا [daḥā] is to spread out. The same Alcamus: الادحي والادحوة والادحية مبيض النعام في الرمل [al-udḥī wa-l-udḥuwwa wa-l-udḥiyya mabīḍ al-naʿām fī al-raml] Udcha, and udchua, and udchia, the ostrich's nest in the sands. Of which Philes [=Manuel Philes, De animalium proprietate (14th c.)] says thus in his Iambics:
Καὶ τὴν καλιὰν τοῖς ποσὶν διαγλύφειν Εἰς ἀνέχουσαν ψάμμον ἐν τῷ δαπέδῳ, [Kai tēn kalian tois posin diaglyphein Eis anechousan psammon en tō dapedō,]

And (they say) that it hollows out its nest with its feet upon raised sand on the ground. But much more fully Aelian, from whom this was adapted, book 14, chapter 7: Καλιὰν ἐργάζεται ταπεινὴν ἐν τῷ δαπέδῳ, τὴν ψάμμον διαγλύψασα τοῖς ποσὶ, καὶ τὸ μὲν μεσαίτατον αὐτῆς κοῖλόν ἐστι· τὰ χείλη δὲ τὰ κύκλῳ ὑψηλὰ ἐργάζεται, ἀποτειχίζουσα τρόπον τινά· ἵνα τὸ ἐκ Διὸς ὕδωρ ἀποστέξῃ, καὶ μὴ εἰσρέῃ τῇ καλιᾷ, καὶ ἐπικλύζῃ τῆς στρουθοῦ τοὺς νεοττοὺς, ὄντας ἁπαλούς. [Kalian ergazetai tapeinēn en tō dapedō, tēn psammon diaglypsasa tois posi, kai to men mesaitaton autēs koilon estin; ta cheilē de ta kyklō hypsēla ergazetai, apoteichizousa tropon tina; hina to ek Dios hydōr apostexē, kai mē eisreē tē kalia, kai epiklyzē tēs strouthou tous neottous, ontas hapalous.] It builds a low nest on the ground, hollowing out the sand with its feet. Its middle is hollow, but it raises the surrounding rims high and, as it were, walls it round, so that those rims may keep out the rain, lest it flow into the nest and wash over the ostrich's still tender chicks. So it is now not obscure why in Arabic it is called ادحي [udḥī] from the sand spread out all around. Note in passing that in Aelian's text ἀποστάξῃ [apostaxē] is wrongly read, and that the true reading is ἀποστέξῃ [apostexē], which has been relegated to the margin. But both Aelian and Philes must also be corrected in the words διαγλύψασα [diaglypsasa] and διαγλύφειν [diaglyphein]. For one should read διαγλάψασα [diaglapsasa] and διαγλάφειν [diaglaphein]. The word is taken from Homer, line 437 [col. 253] of Odyssey δ [delta], about Idothea, daughter of Proteus:
Εὐνὰς δ᾽ ἐν ψαμάθοισι διαγλάψασ᾽ ἁλίῃσιν, [Eunas d' en psamathoisi diaglaps' haliēsin,]

When she had hollowed out beds in the sands of the sea. Where the Scholiasts have: Διαγλάψασα· διακοιλάνασα [Diaglapsasa; diakoilanasa], hollowing out. But διαγλύφειν [diaglyphein] is to engrave, to carve through.

And on the dust they are warmed] In Hebrew תחמם, is warmed; supply each one of the eggs. This is an enallage of number, of which we spoke just now. Others render warms, which does not fit with what precedes [II, 858]: She leaves her eggs, and warms them. For the ostrich does not warm the very eggs it has left. To avoid this difficulty Saint Jerome changed the person thus: When she abandons her eggs on the ground, will you perhaps warm them in the dust? For the verb תחמם can be second person masculine as well as third person feminine. But he added you perhaps of his own, and omitted the conjunction AND, which does not allow this change of person. For it is not correct to say, When she leaves her eggs on the ground, and you will warm them in the dust, for will you warm them in the dust? I have therefore preferred to render and on the dust it is warmed, although תחמם is in Piel, a conjugation which very often has an active meaning, but sometimes also an intransitive one. Further, the eggs, deserted by the mother, are said to be warmed, not with the heat that gives life, but with the heat that corrupts. For the interpreters' view that they are hatched by the heat of the sun alone, or by the warmth of the dust alone, without the mother's help, is a mere dream, which the commentators draw from Isidore, Albertus, Cardano, Vallés, etc. But the Arabs teach that these deserted eggs are corrupted and rot, as will be noted below. Yet, if we believe Damiri, ومن اعاجيب النعامة انها تضع بيضها طولا بحيث لو مد عليه خيط لم يجد لشي منه خروجا عن الاخر ثم تعطي كل بيضة نصيبها من الحضن ان كان كل بدنها لا يشتمل علي عدد بيضها [wa-min aʿājīb al-naʿāma annahā taḍaʿu bayḍahā ṭūlan bi-ḥaythu law mudda ʿalayhi khayṭ lam yajid li-shay minhu khurūjan ʿan al-ākhar thumma tuʿṭī kull bayḍa naṣībahā min al-ḥaḍn in kāna kull badanihā lā yashtamil ʿalī ʿadad bayḍihā] Among the marvels of the ostrich is also this, that it arranges its eggs lengthwise in such a way that, if a thread were stretched over them, not a single one would be found to project beyond another. When this is done, each egg receives its share of her incubation, although her body cannot cover them all. This happens, as they would have it, through the transmission of a power, as in a chain of iron rings, if one is rubbed on a magnet, the rest follow the first.

And she forgets that a foot may crush them] The Greeks have σκορπιεῖ [skorpiei], and the Chaldee תבדרנה, may scatter them; but the Hebrew תזורה is from the verb זור, to crush, not from זרה, to scatter. The Syriac, with no sense at all, has ܘܛܥܝܐ ܕܪܓܠܐ ܕܦܪܚܬܐ ܐܝܬ ܠܗ̇ [וטעיא דרגלא דפרחתא אית לה], And she forgets that she has the foot of a bird: as if for רגל תזורה he had read רגל צפור לה; which is quite beside the point, and indeed false. For the ostrich does not have a toed foot like birds, but a cloven one like quadrupeds. The Philosopher, On the Parts of Animals, book 4, chapter 14: Δίπους μέν ἐστιν, ὡς ὄρνις· διχηλὸς δὲ ὡς τετράπους· οὐ γὰρ δακτύλους ἔχει, ἀλλὰ χηλάς [Dipous men estin, hōs ornis; dichēlos de hōs tetrapous; ou gar daktylous echei, alla chēlas]. It is two-footed, like a bird, but cloven-hoofed, like a quadruped; for it does not have toes, but a cloven hoof. So it truly does not have the foot of a bird. But the Hebrew is plain [col. 254]: She forgets that a foot may crush them; that is, she is so stupid that she does not consider [II, 859] that it may happen that her eggs, which she has left on the ground, are trodden by the feet of wild beasts or of men. As if it made no difference to her whether they are crushed or not. As if Ulysses had not turned aside his plough when, as he was ploughing, his son was laid in the furrow he was drawing.

She deals harshly with her young, as if they were not hers] The Chaldee renders it very differently: שיחנא על בניא דלא דילה, She broods over young that are not hers, that is, over the eggs of others, from which chicks may emerge. The Syriac has ܐܣܓܝܬ [אסגית], she multiplies young not her own. The Arabic follows the same sense, and it describes the habits of the ostrich very well; of it Damir says: متي وجدت بيضة نعامة اخري تحضنها وتنسي بيضها [matā wajadat bayḍat naʿāma ukhrā taḥḍinuhā wa-tansā bayḍahā] If she comes upon the eggs of another ostrich, she broods them and forgets her own. Yet the Hebrew does not bear this rendering. Pagninus [=Santes Pagnino, Latin Bible (1528) and Thesaurus linguae sanctae] has: He makes her forget her young, in which they will not be. This I do not understand. Junius [=Franciscus Junius, of the Tremellius-Junius Latin Bible] has: God, parching, hatches her young by another's work; that is, by the heat of the sun He warms the eggs which the ostrich had laid in the sand, until the chicks are hatched, as he also says in his Notes. For since he saw this asserted about the ostrich by learned men, he tried to bend the Hebrew text in that direction. But the simplest rendering is the one we have given, and it is therefore also the most ancient: She deals harshly with her young. In Hebrew, הקשיח בניה. The verb הקשיח occurs only here and in these words of Isa 63:17. Why hast thou let us stray from thy ways, O Lord, and תקשיח לבנו מיראתך, hardened our heart from thy fear? There the Septuagint has Ἐσκλήρυνας τὰς καρδίας ἡμῶν [Esklērynas tas kardias hēmōn]; and Jerome, Thou hast hardened our heart? Nor do the Syriac and the Arabic differ. For קשח, with Cheth, is the same as הקשה, with He, except that in the former the stronger aspiration seems to intensify the meaning. So also in Arabic قسي [qasā] means to be hard, but قسح [qasaḥa] to be very hard and to be rigid. Hence قساح [qassāḥ] hyena, because it has a rigid neck, not flexible in any way. And رمح قاسح [rumḥ qāsiḥ] is a hard and rigid spear, like the spear of Lausus, of which the Poet speaks in book 10 of the Aeneid:
He comes up, and strikes Dryops from afar with his rigid spear.

Hence, then, applied to the mind, قسح [qasaḥa] or קשח means to be hard and unbending in mind; and הקשיח means either to be hardened or to deal harshly with someone ^{R3}. Accordingly Jerome here has: She was hard toward her young. And Augustine: She hardened herself against her young. And the Greeks: Ἀπεσκλήρυνε τὰ τέκνα αὐτῆς [Apesklēryne ta tekna autēs], that is, τὴν περὶ τὰ τέκνα φυσικὴν στοργήν [tēn peri ta tekna physikēn storgēn]: She hardened her natural affection toward her young, as Olympiodorus rightly explains. To this belong these words of Jeremiah, Lam 4:3: The daughter of my people is cruel, [II, 860] like the ostriches in the desert. So too the fact that the ostrich is called תחמס in Hebrew and ظليم [ẓalīm] in Arabic, that is, impious, unjust, as we have already shown above ^{c)}. That the masculine verb הקשיח is used here for the feminine will surprise only someone who does not know how frequent this change of gender is in Hebrew idiom, especially with animals. Thus Isa 14:11. תחתיך יצע רמה ומכסיך תולעה, Beneath thee the worm is spread, and the maggot covers thee. There the nouns are feminine, but the verbs masculine. Conversely, in Exod 8:2 [var. 6.] ותעל הצפרדע, And the frog came up; and in verse 14 [var. 16], ותהי הכנים, And there was the louse: feminine verbs are joined to masculine nouns. Kimchi [=David Kimḥi (Radak), Sefer ha-Shorashim], on Isaiah, says this is the custom of Scripture [col. 255] when it speaks not of this or that animal, but על דרך כלל, universally, of the whole species, as here of the ostrich. Her young, in Hebrew בניה, her sons, that is, the eggs from which chicks would have emerged had she brooded them. They are therefore called sons δυνωτικῶς [dynōtikōs]. Compare that line of Martial, book 9, Epigram 42:
What you waste with your fingers, Ponticus, is a man.

As if they were not hers] In Hebrew, ללא לה. In full it would be כאשר לא יהיו לה, as in Job 10:19. כאשר לא הייתי, As if I had not been ^{R4}. But in this book the style is sometimes very concise, because it is not prose but verse. And this antithesis has its own charm: her young, as though not hers. Compare that of Paul, 1 Cor 7:30: Οἱ κλαίοντες ὡς μὴ κλαίοντες, καὶ οἱ χαίροντες ὡς μὴ χαίροντες [Hoi klaiontes hōs mē klaiontes, kai hoi chairontes hōs mē chairontes], etc. Those who weep as though not weeping, and those who rejoice as though not rejoicing, etc. And Heb 11:27 Τὸν γὰρ ἀόρατον ὡς ὁρῶν [Ton gar aoraton hōs horōn]: As seeing him who is invisible.

She labors in vain, without fear] Mothers are said to have labored in vain when they bear children who will not live. So Isa 65:23. They shall not labor in vain, nor bring forth for trouble. So in the Agamemnon of Aeschylus the vultures grieve over their stolen young, δεμνιοτήρη πόνον ὀρταλίχων ὀλέσαντες [demniotērē ponon ortalichōn olesantes], having lost the labor they had spent in guarding the nest of their chicks. In this same sense Job writes that the ostrich labors in vain when it neglects the eggs it has laid, not without labor: namely, because it is without fear. Not without all fear, for the ostrich is a most timid animal. Accordingly, among the Arabs one of the various names of the ostrich is اجفيل [ijfīl] igphil, as if you were to say timid. Alcamus: الاجفيل الجبن والظليم ينفر من كل شي [al-ijfīl al-jabān wa-al-ẓalīm yanfiru min kull shī], Igphil, that is, timid; also the male ostrich, which flees for any cause whatever. There is also an Arabic proverb, اجبن [II, 861] نعامة من اجبن [ajban naʿāma min ajban], more timid than an ostrich: خافت انها لانها وذلك ابدا اليه ترجع لا موضع من [khāfat annahā li-annahā wa-dhālika abadan ilayhi tarjiʿ lā mawḍiʿ min], and this because, when it flees from some place out of fear, it never returns there. So Damir in the section On Proverbs. But here the ostrich is said to be devoid of fear, because it lacks that provident fear by which parents are driven to look out for their young. This fear springs from love. Ovid in the Epistle of Penelope:
Love is a thing full of anxious fear.
And this fear always keeps parents anxious and troubled. Hence that father in the Comic poet:
I, because my son has not come back, what things I think of, and by what things I am now troubled: lest he has caught cold, or fallen somewhere, or broken something.

But the ostrich, because it does not love, likewise does not fear for its young. As soon as it has left the nest, it forgets its own eggs and sits on those of others with the same affection as on its own. But, you will say, in Aelian (Hist. book 14, ch. 7) the ostrich is described as ἐρῶσα τῶν νεοττῶν ἰσχυρῶς, καὶ διψῶσα αὐτῶν τῆς συνουσίας [erōsa tōn neottōn ischyrōs, kai dipsōsa autōn tēs synousias], loving its chicks intensely, and thirsting for their company, that is, supremely eager for it. So much so that, returning from foraging, although it finds the nest fenced about by the hunter with iron points, nevertheless νικωμένη ὑπὸ τοῦ ἱμέρου, καὶ οἰστρουμένη [nikōmenē hypo tou himerou, kai oistroumenē], overcome by longing for them, and roused as if by a gadfly, it rushes with spread wings, running and screeching, into the midst of the iron, and so, pierced by its own onrush, perishes miserably. I reply that, of all the writers who have treated the ostrich, Aelian alone reports this; and that he could have been deceived in this report just as in what precedes it, that the ostrich lays ὑπὲρ τὰ ὀγδοή- [col. 256] κοντα [hyper ta ogdoēkonta], more than eighty eggs, whereas Alkazuinius reckons only twenty, and Leo Africanus and Marmolius only ten or twelve. Or, if the story is true, that it is the effect not of love but of stupidity that the ostrich rushes onto the iron with so blind an impulse. Of this stupidity there follows in Job:

Because God has deprived her of wisdom, nor has he imparted understanding to her] For although wisdom and understanding, if we wish to speak properly, belong only to human beings, who are endowed with reason, they are nevertheless also attributed to brute animals in Scripture. Thus the serpent is said to be the φρονιμώτατος [phronimōtatos] of all animals, Gen 3:1. And Christ himself bids us imitate its prudence, Matt 10:16 Isaiah too sets before us the example of the ox and the ass, which know their owner and their master's crib, Isa 1:3 Jeremiah sets before us the stork, which knows her appointed times, and the turtledove, the crane and the swallow, which observe the time of their coming, Jer 8:7. And Solomon sets before us the ant, so that, having considered her ways, we may be wise, Prov. [II, 862] VI, 6. Indeed, although he was by far the wisest of men, he nevertheless praises four small creatures as חכמים מחכמים, exceedingly wise: namely, besides the ants, the choerogryllii, the locusts and the stellions, Prov 30:24. But certain brute animals are said to be exceedingly wise: 1. Because they are as wise as is necessary for their own preservation. 2. Because they excel among the other brutes in this wisdom of theirs. Yet this wisdom falls short of human wisdom by many degrees, since it lacks the light of reason and is determined to a single end. But here God is said to have denied even this wisdom, such as it is, to the ostrich. He alone is the author not only of human ingenuity but also of that of the brutes. To this they refer what is found in Job 38:36 according to the Chaldee and the Vulgate: Who gave the cock understanding? that is, no one other than God. Further, the Hebrew says of the ostrich כי השה אלוה חכמה, literally because God made her forget wisdom. For from נשה, to forget, the Hiphil is השה. But the Greeks have Κατεσιώπησεν αὐτῇ ὁ Θεὸς σοφίαν [Katesiōpēsen autē ho Theos sophian], God made wisdom silent for her. And the Syriac has ܐܣܓܝ [אסגי], and the Arabic أكثر [akthara], he multiplied, in a sense not only different but entirely contrary. The Greeks, that is, read instead of השה, with He, חשה, with Cheth, he was silent or he made silent. And the Syriac, followed by the Arabic, inserting a Gimel, read השגה, he multiplied. But the Chaldee rightly has אנשיה, he made her forget wisdom. Now God is said to bring about forgetfulness of things past when a great change takes place: for instance, if prosperity follows adversity, or adversity prosperity. Thus Joseph, raised to the height of honours in Egypt, named his firstborn Manasseh, from forgetting. For God, he says, has made me forget my former toil, Gen 41:51. Conversely, in the Babylonian captivity Jeremiah laments that God has caused the solemn feasts and sabbaths to be forgotten in Zion, Lam 2:6. What is said here, that God made the ostrich forget wisdom, is not to be taken in that sense, as though she had previously remembered it and some change had occurred in her nature. For here to forget is nothing other than not to remember. This forgetfulness is not privative but negative, just as Moses calls the state before the creation of light darkness, not as a privation of light but as a mere negation, Gen 1:3. Accordingly, in the following hemistich there is added ἐξηγητικῶς [exēgētikōs], ולא חלק לה בבינה, And he did not impart to her understanding, or prudence. Thus made her forget means did not impart. חלק, commonly to divide, here means to impart, like the Greek νέμειν [nemein]. Symmachus therefore rightly has Οὐκ ἔνειμεν αὐτῇ σύνεσιν [Ouk eneimen autē synesin], where the Elders have Οὐκ ἐπεμέρισεν αὐτῇ ἐν τῇ συνέσει [Ouk epemerisen autē en tē synesei], He did not distribute to her, or He did not give her a share in understanding. As it is said to Simon Magus in Actor. VIII, 21. Οὐκ ἔστι σοι μερὶς, οὐδὲ κλῆρος ἐν τῷ λόγῳ τούτῳ· [Ouk esti soi meris, oude klēros en tō logō toutō] You have neither part [col. 257] nor lot in this matter; Acts 8:21.

There are some who hold that part of the eggs is neglected by the ostrich neither through imprudence nor through carelessness or ἀστοργίαν [astorgian], but by deliberate design, and that she does this [II, 863] with discrimination, rejecting only τὰ ὑπηνέμια [ta hypēnemia], or those which must be kept for feeding the chicks. Aelian, History, book 4, chapter 37: Ἡ στρουθὸς ἡ μεγάλη ὠὰ μὲν ἀποτίκτει πολλὰ, οὐ πάντα δὲ ἀποκύει, ἀλλ᾽ ἀποκρίνει τὰ ἄγονα, τοῖς δὲ ἐγκάρποις ἐπῳάζει, καὶ ἐκ μὲν τούτων τοὺς νεοττοὺς ἐξέλεψεν, ἐκεῖνα δὲ τὰ ἐκφαυλισθέντα τούτοις τροφὴν παρατίθησιν. [Hē strouthos hē megalē ōa men apotiktei polla, ou panta de apokyei, alla apokrinei ta agona, tois de enkarpois epōazei, kai ek men toutōn tous neottous exelepsen, ekeina de ta ekphaulisthenta toutois trophēn paratithēsin.] Although the ostrich lays many eggs, she does not use all of them for hatching, but sets apart the sterile ones and broods only on the fertile ones. When she has hatched the chicks from these, she sets the spoiled eggs before them as food. And Philes, in the place cited above:

Ὠῶν δὲ συχνῶν εὑρεθεῖσαν ἐργάτιν Τὰ μὴ καθαρά γε τῆς γονῆς ἀποκρίνειν· Ὅσους γὰρ ἐξέλεψεν ἡ ζέσις τόκους, Ἐν τοῖς ἀποῤῥεύσασι κυλίνδροις τρέφειν. [Ōōn de sychnōn heuretheisan ergatin / Ta mē kathara ge tēs gonēs apokrinein· / Hosous gar exelepsen hē zesis tokous, / En tois aporrheusasi kylindrois trephein.]

And since it is found to be the producer of many eggs, it (is said) to separate from the brood those that are impure, and to nourish with the flowing cylinders as many chicks as the heat has hatched. So he calls, very improperly, the wind-eggs, whose fluid, and the shell flowing away, nourish the chicks. Damir: يقال انها تقسم بيضها ثلاثا فمنه ما تحضنه ومنه ما تجعل صغارة غذ ومنه ما تفتحه وتجعله في الهوا حتي يتعفن ويتولد دودا فتتغذي به فراخها اذا خرجت من البيض [yuqāl annahā taqsim bayḍahā thalāthan fa-minhu mā taḥḍunuhu wa-minhu mā tajʿal ṣighāra ghadh wa-minhu mā taftaḥuhu wa-tajʿaluhu fī al-hawā ḥattī yataʿaffan wa-yatawallad dūdan fa-tataghadhdhī bihi firākhuhā idhā kharajat min al-bayḍ] It is said to divide its eggs into three parts, so that some of them are those on which it sits; some also, from whose yolk it is fed; and some, finally, which it opens and exposes to the air until they rot and worms are produced from them, by which its chicks are fed when they have been hatched from the egg. Alkazuinius: واذا باضت يبيض عشرين بيضة او اكثر فيجعلها ثلاثة اقسام تدفن ثلثها في التراب وتترك ثلثها في الشمس وتخضن ثلثها فاذا اخرجت فراخها كسرت ما كان في الشمس وغذتها بما فيها من الرطوبة التي ذوبتها الشمس ورقتها فاذا اشتدت فراخها وقويت اخرجت المدفون وفتحت لها ثقبا فتجمع عليها الذباب والبق والنمل وغيرها من فرعت فغذت تقوي ان الي فراخها فتاكلها الهوام [wa-idhā bāḍat yabīḍ ʿishrīn bayḍa aw akthar fa-yajʿaluhā thalāthat aqsām tadfin thuluthahā fī al-turāb wa-tatruk thuluthahā fī al-shams wa-takhḍin thuluthahā fa-idhā akhrajat firākhahā kasarat mā kāna fī al-shams wa-ghadhdhathā bi-mā fīhā min al-ruṭūba allatī dhawwabathā al-shams wa-raqqathā fa-idhā ishtaddat firākhuhā wa-qawiyat akhrajat al-madfūn wa-fataḥat lahā thuqban fa-tajammaʿ ʿalayhā al-dhubāb wa-al-baqq wa-al-naml wa-ghayruhā min frʿt fghdht tqwy an ilā firākhihā fa-taʾkuluhā al-hawāmm] [col. 258] When it lays eggs — and it lays twenty or more — it divides them into three parts: one of these it buries in the earth, one it exposes to the sun, and on one it sits. And when the chicks have hatched, it breaks the part that was in the sun and feeds the chicks with the fluid they contain, [II, 864] after it has been liquefied and softened by the sun. And when the chicks grow strong and sturdy, it digs up the buried eggs and pierces them, so that flies, bugs, ants and similar little creatures gather to them, on which the chicks feed until, having become stronger, they run and feed themselves. But these things are closer to fables, since they attribute to the animal not only prudence but also foresight; yet that it is most stupid will be evident from what I am about to say.

1. Other animals choose foods suited to their nature; this one devours without any discrimination whatever presents itself: iron, bones, glass, stones, clods of earth, coals, glowing embers, gems hanging from the ears of bystanders; and it is said not only to swallow these but also to digest them. Pliny, book 10, chapter 1: Of a wondrous nature in digesting what it has devoured without discrimination. Aelian, book 14, chapter 7, says that stones are found in the belly of a slain one, ὥσπερ οὖν καταπιοῦσα ἡ στρουθὸς ἐν τῷ ἐχίνῳ φυλάττει, καὶ πέττει τῷ χρόνῳ [hōsper oun katapiousa hē strouthos en tō echinō phylattei, kai pettei tō chronō], which, having swallowed them and kept them in its omasum, it at length digests. Porta coeli fol. 22. d.: כתב אבן רשד כי בהלעיטה את הזהב הוא נתך בגופה מחמם יותר מן האש בסגולה שלהם, Averroës wrote that it melts swallowed gold in its body, as if it were hotter than fire, through a property implanted in it. Alkazuinius: ياكل الحصاة فتذوب في قانصته حتي يصير كالما بالخاصية خلقها الله فيه [yaʾkul al-ḥaṣāh fa-tadhūb fī qāniṣatihi ḥattī yaṣīr ka-l-mā bi-l-khāṣṣiyya khalaqahā allāh fīhi] It devours stones and melts them in its stomach until they become like water, through a faculty placed in it by God. And a little later: وايضا يبلع الجمر ولا يضرها [wa-ayḍan yablaʿ al-jamr wa-lā yaḍurruhā] It also devours coals, which do it no harm. Likewise: وتحمي صنجة ماية دينار من الحديد حتي تحمر وترمي الي النعامة فتبلعها وتسترها [wa-tuḥmā ṣanjat māyat dīnār min al-ḥadīd ḥattā taḥmarr wa-turmā ilā al-naʿāma fa-tablaʿuhā wa-tasturuhā] And an iron weight of a hundred denarii is heated until red-hot and thrown to the ostrich, which devours it and stores it away. So also Damir: وتتبلع العظم الصلب والحجر والمدر والحديد وتذيبه ^{d)} كالماء [wa-tatabalaʿ al-ʿaẓm al-ṣulb wa-al-ḥajar wa-al-madar wa-al-ḥadīd wa-tudhībuhu ^{d)} ka-l-māʾ] And it devours hard bones, and stones, and clods, and iron, which it liquefies like water. Likewise: واذا رات في اذن صغير لولوة خطفتها [wa-idhā raʾat fī udhn ṣaghīr luʾluʾa khaṭifathā] And when it sees a small pearl in an ear, it snatches it. And again: وتتبلع الجمر فيكون جوفها هو العامل في اطفايه [II, 865] ولا يكون الجمر عاملا في احراقة وفي ذلك اعجوبتان احدا [col. 259] هما التغذي بما لا يتغذي به والثانية الاستمرا والهضم [wa-tatabalaʿ al-jamr fa-yakūn jawfuhā huwa al-ʿāmil fī iṭfāyih [II, 865] wa-lā yakūn al-jamr ʿāmilan fī iḥrāqih wa-fī dhālika uʿjūbatān aḥad [col. 259] humā al-taghadhdhī bi-mā lā yutaghadhdhā bihi wa-al-thāniya al-istimrā wa-al-haḍm] It also swallows embers, and its body is effective in extinguishing them, but the embers are not effective in burning it. In this there is a double marvel: one, that it is nourished by things that do not nourish; the other, their digestion and concoction. So they say, but, as usual, hyperbolically exaggerated. Aelian says stones are found in its belly which it has swallowed and digested, which is a remarkable ἐναντιολογία [enantiologia]. Alexander of Aphrodisias, in the Preface to Aristotle's Problems, expressly denies that iron is digested by the ostrich. And Albertus asserts that the stones it has greedily devoured it afterwards spits out, that is, ejects through the mouth. And Ulysses Aldrovandi [=Ulisse Aldrovandi, Ornithologia (1599–1603)] says it swallows bits of iron which it excretes again undigested. And Gesner [=Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium], after saying that it devours whatever it touches, linen, iron, stones, says: But these remain undigested and whole in its stomach. And if they are too many, they finally bring the animal to death or to wasting, as has appeared in dissected ones.

2. The second proof of its stupidity is that the ostrich, having hidden its head among bushes, thinks that it is entirely concealed. Pliny: No less (remarkable) is the stupidity, in so great a height of body, of those who, when they have hidden their necks in a bush, think that they are concealed. Oppian, after telling this very thing of the bubalis, Halieutica book 4, line 630:
Τοῖα δὲ καὶ Λιβύης πτερόεν βοτὸν ἀγκυλόδειρον Νήπια τεχνάζει· — — [Toia de kai Libyēs pteroen boton ankyloderon / Nēpia technazei]

Such childish tricks does the winged, crook-necked beast of Libya also practise. Tertullian, On the Veiling of Virgins, chapter 17: They say that this bird, when it has to hide, buries only its head, plainly and wholly, in a thicket, and leaves the rest of itself in the open. Claudian, Against Eutropius, book 2:
— — it stands with eyes shut, its head ridiculously turned back, and believes that what it does not itself see is hidden. —

Damir: من حمق النعامة انها اذا ادركها القناص ادخلت راسها في كثيب رمل تقدر انها قد استخفت منه [min ḥumq al-naʿāma annahā idhā adrakahā al-qannāṣ adkhalat raʾsahā fī kathīb raml taqdiru annahā qad istakhfat minhu] Among the follies of the ostrich is this: when the hunter pursues it, it thrusts its head into a heap of sand, thinking that it is hidden from him. Or انها قد استحصنت منه [annahā qad istaḥṣanat minhu] that it is safe from him, as another copy has it. Yet, since men's judgements vary, here too the bird has a defender of its folly in Diodorus, in these words: Ἐπειδὰν δὲ περικατάληπτον ᾖ, τὴν κεφαλὴν εἴς τινα θάμνον, ἢ τοιαύτην σκέπην ἀποκρύπτεται, οὐχ᾽, ὡς οἴονταί τινες. ἀφροσύνῃ, [II, 866] καὶ νωθρότητι ψυχῆς, διὰ τὸ μὴ βλέπειν ἑτέρους, μηδ᾽ αὐτὸ βλέπεσθαι διαλάμβανον ὑφ᾽ ἑτέρων· ἀλλὰ, διὰ τὸ τοῦ σώματος ἔχειν τοῦτο τὸ μέρος ἀσθενέστατον, σκέπην αὐτῷ πρὸς σωτηρίαν περιποιεῖν. [Epeidan de perikatalēpton ē, tēn kephalēn eis tina thamnon, ē toiautēn skepēn apokryptetai, ouch, hōs oiontai tines, aphrosynē kai nōthrotēti psychēs, dia to mē blepein heterous, mēd' auto blepesthai dialambanon hyph' heterōn; alla, dia to tou sōmatos echein touto to meros asthenestaton, skepēn autō pros sōtērian peripoiein.] When it is on the point of being caught, it hides its head in some shrub or other such hiding place. It does not do so because, out of stupidity or dullness of mind, as some think, it concludes from the fact that it does not see others that it is not itself seen by others, but because this part of its body is the weakest, it protects itself with this cover for its safety. But Tertullian refutes this excuse in a few words: While it is secure in its head, it is caught, naked where it is larger, whole along with its head. He means that the head is hidden in vain while the rest of the body lies open to the hunter; once that is caught, or mortally struck, the head cannot escape.

3. And this animal is also plainly most stupid, if what Strabo [col. 260] says in book 16 is true, about the method of hunting it practised among the Struthophagi: Θηρεύουσι δὲ αὐτοὺς οἱ μὲν τόξοις, οἱ δὲ ταῖς δοραῖς τῶν στρουθῶν σκεπασθέντες· τὴν μὲν δεξιὰν καλύπτουσι τῷ τραχηλιμαίῳ μέρει, καὶ κινοῦσιν οὕτως ὥσπερ τὰ ζῶα κινεῖται τοῖς τραχήλοις· τῇ δὲ ἀριστερᾷ σπέρμα προχέουσιν ἀπὸ πήρας παρηρτημένης, καὶ τούτῳ δελεάσαντες τὰ ζῶα εἰς φάραγγας συνωθοῦσιν. [Thēreuousi de autous hoi men toxois, hoi de tais dorais tōn strouthōn skepasthentes; tēn men dexian kalyptousi tō trachēlimaiō merei, kai kinousin houtōs hōsper ta zōa kineitai tois trachēlois; tē de aristera sperma procheousin apo pēras parērtēmenēs, kai toutō deleasantes ta zōa eis pharangas synōthousin.] Some hunt the ostriches with bows, others covered with their skins: for they clothe the right hand in the skin of the neck and move it as the animals move their necks, while with the left they scatter seed taken from a bag hanging at their side; luring the birds with this, they drive them into ravines. For although the human form differs immeasurably from the shape of the ostrich, yet these foolish birds, through dullness of mind, let themselves be deceived by this trick. Nor was there any need here for the brush of Zeuxis, who brought onto the stage grapes painted with such success that birds flew to them; nor for the chisel of Myron, whose heifer kindled bulls to love: since they were lured by this rough sketch of their own figure, however crude and shapeless.

4. The fourth sign of stupidity in the ostrich is the very thing that Job presses: that it abandons its eggs and is unmindful of them. Isaiah's ἐπιφώνημα [epiphōnēma] is well known, as if about something impossible, Isa 49:15. Can a woman forget her offspring, so as not to have compassion on the son of her womb? And the same affection toward offspring has been implanted by nature in the other animals, so that the species may be preserved; it is attributed even to the cetaceans, which are by far the most savage of all animals, Lam 4:3. But the ostrich is here excepted, which leaves its eggs on the ground, etc. Hence Damir above: When it leaves the nest to seek food, if it finds the eggs of another ostrich, تحضنه وتنسى بيضها [taḥḍunuhu wa-tansā bayḍahā] it broods on them and forgets its own. And Leo Africanus, book 9: It lays its eggs, ten or twelve in number, in the sand, etc. And since it has a very short memory, it immediately forgets the place. Therefore the female, coming upon these eggs, whether her own or another's, sits on them and warms them. The same is found in Marmol. [II, 867] 5. Finally, among the Arabs, to whom this bird is very well known, we have noted that احمق من النعامة [aḥmaq min al-naʿāma] more foolish than an ostrich is said for "most foolish." The very build of its body amply shows this. For it has a very small head and almost no brain. Hence in Arabic it is called صعون [ṣaʿwan] sivvan, that is, الدقيق العنق والصغير الراس او العام [al-daqīq al-ʿunuq wa-al-ṣaghīr al-rās aw al-ʿām] thin of neck and small of head, or of crown. It is also called انقخ [anqakh] ankach, that is, قليل الدماغ [qalīl al-dimāgh] of little brain. So Alcamus. For this reason Heliogabalus served the heads of six hundred ostriches at a single dinner, so that their little brains might be eaten. So many were needed for there to be plenty for the guests, since individual ostriches have hardly any brain. Further, the head of the ostrich, carried on a long thin neck, cannot be steady. That is why they call the animal itself نغض [nighḍ] nigd, because نغض [naghaḍa] nagada means to nod the head. Again Alcamus: نغض اسم الظليم معرفة للجوال منه [nighḍ ism al-ẓalīm maʿrifa lil-jawwāl minhu] Nigd, a name of the ostrich, given to it from its agitation. And on the same word Damir: الظليم سمي بذلك لانه يحرك راسه [al-ẓalīm summiya bi-dhālika li-annahu yuḥarriku rasahu] The ostrich is so called because it moves its head. With such agitation of the head the imaginative faculty can hardly be steady and keep to its own level. And since the ear, even in brute animals, is in its own way the sense of learning, in the ostrich stupidity is increased by deafness, which is natural to it. Khalawayh, in the book ليس [laysa] Laisa, or There is not (which we said is On things that are lacking to someone, or somewhere): ليس في الدنيا حيوان لا يسمع الا النعام [laysa fī al-dunyā ḥayawān lā yasmaʿu illā al-naʿām] There is no animal in the world (no perfect animal) that does not hear, except the ostrich. [col. 261] Leo Africanus, book 9: The ostrich is a simple and deaf animal. Marmol: El abestruez es simple, y sordò, que no oye cosa ninguna. All this sheds light on these words of Job: God has deprived her of wisdom, etc. It remains to explain the last words of the sacred writer, who closes the description of the ostrich thus:

At the time when it lifts itself on high, it laughs at the horse and its rider] The sense is that God so deprived this bird of wisdom that he nevertheless provided for its safety and preservation, since it is not easy for a man, even a horseman, to overtake it. At the time when: כעת, or κατὰ καιρὸν [kata kairon], when the time has come; so the Greeks, Jerome, Pagninus, the Genevans, etc., which is how it seems to be taken in Num 23:23. Otherwise כעת is more often joined with what follows, as כעת מחר, at the time of tomorrow, 1 Sam 9:16, and passim; כעת מנחת ערב, at the time of the evening offering, Dan 9:21; כעת הראשון יקל, At the time when the first was light, Isa 8:23. So here I prefer, with the Chaldee, to take it as At the time when it lifts itself on high, it laughs, etc., because the two hemistichs cohere better this way. It lifts itself on high] In Hebrew במרום תמריא. Because the word תמריא occurs only here, the ancient interpreters explain it variously. [II, 868] The Syriac has ܬܬܬܪܝܡ ܐܝܟ ܕܩܠܐ [תתתרים איך דקלא], and the Arabic likewise ترتفع مثل النخلة [tartafiʿ mithl al-nakhla], It is raised up like a palm, as if תמריא thamri alluded to תמר thamar, that is, to the palm. This is absurd, since in תמריא the Thau is servile. The Chaldee, however, has טיסא, it flies. And the old Scholiast on this passage: Ἐν τῇ πτήσει τὸ θαῤῥεῖν ἔχουσα ἵπταται [En tē ptēsei to tharrhein echousa hiptatai], Trusting in its flight it flies. Jerome better: it raises its wings. The Seventy best of all: ὑψώσει [hypsōsei], it will be lifted up. For the ostrich does not fly, since it is incapable of flight; rather it raises its wings on high, or rather it is itself lifted on high. That is, when hunters approach the nest, it rises from its resting place and towers up beyond belief through the tallness of its stature and the stretching out of its neck, which is aptly signified by the word תמריא. For it is the future of Hiphil, and the Kal is מרא mara; which, with the letters transposed, seems to have been formed from ראם raam, that is, to be high. For we have proved elsewhere ^{e)} that רום rum and ראם raam mean the same ^{R5}. So by these words, it is raised on high, the tallness of the ostrich's stature is commended, about which writers say much. Aristotle, On the Parts of Animals, at the end of the fourth book: Τὸ μέγεθος οὐκ ὄρνιθος ἔχει, ἀλλὰ τετράποδος [To megethos ouk ornithos echei, alla tetrapodos]· It has the size not of a bird but of a quadruped. Diodorus, book 2: Τὸ μέγεθος ἔχουσι νεογονεῖ καμήλῳ παραπλήσιον [To megethos echousi neogonei kamēlō paraplēsion]· It has nearly the size of a newborn camel. Oppian, in the third book of the Cynegetica:
Τῆς ἤτοι μέγεθος μὲν ὑπέρβιον, ὅσσον ὕπερθεν Νώτοις εὐρυτάτοισι φέρειν νεοθήλεα κοῦρον· [Tēs ētoi megethos men hyperbion, hosson hyperthen / Nōtois eurytatoisi pherein neothēlea kouron·]

Whose size is immense, so that on its broad back it could carry a newborn boy. Pliny: They exceed the height of a horseman sitting on a horse. Albertus: The ostrich is about five or six feet tall from the feet to the back; it has a very long neck, etc. Therefore the Arabs call it هيق [hayq] heic and هيقم [hayqam] heicam from the length of its neck, and اسقف [usquf] ascaph from its height. This is also what they call the bishops of the Christians, but there the word is derived from the Greek. And of a plant, استرال [istarāl] isterala means to grow tall like the chick of an ostrich, which in Arabic is called رال [rāl] raal. [II, 869] The ostrich, then, raising itself so high, laughs at the horse and its rider. [col. 262] Laughs, that is, scorns, as the Greek Scholiast has it: Καταφρονοῦσα ἵππου σὺν τῷ ἀναβάτῃ διὰ τὴν ἰσχὺν, ὥς φασι, καὶ τὸ μέγεθος [kataphronousa hippou syn tō anabatē dia tēn ischyn, hōs phasi, kai to megethos]. Despising the horse with its rider, on account of its strength, as they say, and its size. Rightly, except that the ostrich should have been said to scorn horse and horseman not in reliance on its strength but on its speed. Hence Pliny: They exceed the height of a horseman sitting on a horse, and surpass him in speed. And Xenophon, in book 1 of the Anabasis, says that the horsemen of Cyrus caught wild asses and roe deer in Arabia, but could in no way overtake the ostriches: Στρουθὸν δὲ οὐδεὶς ἔλαβεν· οἱ δὲ διώξαντες τῶν ἱππέων ταχὺ ἐπαύοντο· πολὺ γὰρ ἀπέσπα αποφεύγουσα [strouthon de oudeis elaben; hoi de diōxantes tōn hippeōn tachy epauonto; poly gar apespa apopheugousa]. No one caught an ostrich; and those who pursued it soon gave up, for in its flight it drew far ahead. This is remarkable in an army equipped with many thousands of horsemen. It is said, indeed, that in Africa, among the breed of horses called Arabian, some are found that can overtake an ostrich in running, but very few, and these of immense price. Marmol, book 1, chapter 23: Cavallos Barbaros son llamados en toda Europa los, que vienen de Berberia: mas ay una especie de cavallos en Africa, y en Egypto, y en las Arabias, y en toda Asia, que llaman cavallos Arabes, que son de casta de cavallos salvages, que se crian por los desiertos de Arabia, etc. Son est rañamente ligeros, y la mayor experiencia, que se haze de su ligereza es quando alcançan una fiera llamada Lamte, o a un abestruz. Porque este tal cavallos es apreciado en mil ducados de oro, o en cien camellos. Mas ay pocos dellos en Berberia. That is: Throughout Europe the horses brought from Barbary are called Barbary horses; but in Africa, Egypt, Arabia and all Asia there is a breed of horses which they call Arabian, descended from those bred in the deserts of Arabia, etc. They are wonderfully swift, and there is no greater proof of their speed than when they overtake the wild beast called the Lamte, or an ostrich. Therefore such a horse is valued at a thousand gold ducats, or a hundred camels. But in Barbary there are few such. And certainly this is the common opinion of the Arabs, that there is no animal which surpasses the ostrich in running. On this point these words of Alkazuinius are explicit: لا يصبقها شي من الحيوانات [lā yaṣbiquhā shay min al-ḥayawānāt] None of the animals outruns it. How this comes about we have shown above ^{f)}: that, using its wings as a sail, it swims, as it were, in the air. Hence Oppian, Cynegetica book 3, verse 500:
Ἠέρος ὑψιπόροισιν ἐπιπλώουσι κελεύθοις, [Ēeros hypsiporoisin epiplōousi keleuthois,]
They swim along the lofty paths of the air. And shortly after, [II, 870] Αὐτοῖσιν φορέουσιν ἴσον τάχος οἰωνοῖσιν, [Autoisin phoreousin ison tachos oiōnoisin,]

They are of equal speed with the birds themselves. Accordingly the Arabs coined many words to express this. Thus of the ostrich, زازا [zāzā] zaza means to flow rather than walk, with head, wings and tail raised; رفرف [rafrafa] raphrapha, to run while flapping the wings, like the Talmudic רפרף riphreph; كحص [kaḥaṣa] chahatsa, to go so swiftly as almost to escape the sight. And for this very reason the ostrich is called عصوف [ʿaṣūf], that is, whirlwind, and by other names, at least ten, derived from the rapidity of its running ^{R6}. Indeed it spurs itself on to run with certain bony spikes which lie hidden under its wings and serve it as spurs. On these it would be easy to adduce much more; but to set this out point by point is not the business of the present place, and it is enough for us to have explained the meaning of the Sacred Writer.

notes.text: Parallel passages (παράλληλα [parallēla]) from the Arab poets and their commentators will be supplied by SCHULTENS in his Commentar. on the passage, p. 1120, 1121, 1122, who should by all means be read, since you will also find there the opinions of others weighed. Nor will you regret comparing SHAW, Itinerar. p. 388 ff., German trans., Leipzig 1765. He illustrates the whole passage of Job with what he himself observed, and confirms by his own testimony what Bochart brought forward from the books of the Arabs. The fable of the ostrich hatching its eggs by the mere gaze of its eyes is reported from Giauhari [=al-Jawharī, al-Ṣiḥāḥ] by WANSLEBEN in his Itinerarium, edited by Paulus [=H. E. G. Paulus, Clavis über die Psalmen (1791) and Clavis über den Jesaias (1793)] in the Sylloge of Itineraries, vol. 3, p. 186. Nor should what Paulus remarked on it in the Notes at the end of the book, p. 395, be passed over.

notes.label: R3

notes.text: But ALB. SCHULTENS, p. 1126, renders it more correctly: it urges itself on to running. For the verb مري [marā] means he drove a horse to a faster run by striking it with the whip. Giauhari: مريت الفرس اذا استخرجت ما عنده من الجري بسوط او غيره [maraytu al-faras idhā istakhrajtu mā ʿindahu min al-jary bi-sawṭ aw ghayrihi] One says מריח אלפרש I urged the horse, when I draw out, by applying the whip, or something else (spurs), whatever it has in running. This verb is indeed most aptly used by the Hebrew poet. For the ostrich, as Shaw [=Thomas Shaw, Travels (1738)] testifies (p. 387, German trans.), has under its wings a small claw with which it wounds itself as it runs harder, and so draws blood. Bochart too notes this very thing below, at the end of our chapter.
